newsitem.title: GERMANY: BASF cool on purchases after Sandoz unit buy.
newsitem.headline: BASF cool on purchases after Sandoz unit buy.

text.p: German chemicals group BASF AG, fresh from buying parts of Swiss group Sandoz AG's herbicides business, on Tuesday said it was not eyeing other purchases soon but would not rule out takeovers.

BASF in September said it had acquired the U.S.-Canadian corn herbicides business from Sandoz AG for $695 million plus about $83 million in net working capital. The Swiss company needed to sell parts of its business in order to merge with its rival Ciba-Geigy AG to form Norvartis.
Meanwhile its German rival AgrEvo GmbH said it still planned to make further acquisitions while Bayer AG said there was currently no need to take action at the moment.

On Tuesday the United States Federal Trade Commission agreed to the multi-billion dollar merger of the two giants, prompting queries whether German companies were possibly considering similar mergers or were considering takeovers more actively.
"I know of no concrete plans, but we have also said that we do not rule out making any other acquisitions," BASF spokesman Matthias Hensel said.
The purchase of the business from Sandoz was designed to help "fill a geographic hole in North America," he added.
BASF remains relatively weak in the insecticides area, Hensel said. The grouup was also still relatively weak in Asia as compared with its presence in Latin America and Europe.
BASF said that the closing for the Sandoz takeover would take place before the end of this year.
Asia and Latin America are considered to be the best potential growth markets for crop protection groups.

At the same time Gerhard Prante, chief executive at AgrEvo, the crop protection company run jointly by Hoechst AG and Schering AG, said his company was still actively looking for cooperations or takeovers.
Asked about specific targets, Prante told Reuters: "Do not limit your imagination," but declined to give more specific information on areas or the timing of any move.
As part of AgrEvo's efforts to improve operating results, where it currently ranks last among the world's top five crop protection groups, Prante said more divestments may be planned.
A spokesman at Bayer said the group was constantly observing the market but said, "There is currently no need to take any action." Bayer has said it prefers to grow through its own products.

"We have our own plans in the U.S. and we have several products in the pipeline," the Bayer spokesman said. He added that these plans had precluded Bayer from showing much interest in the Sandoz business.
AgrEvo currently beats out national rivals Bayer and BASF but clearly lags Swiss giant Norvatis, Prante said.
